cues.text: A Girl's Plea
In 1657, at the Benedictine monastery of Our Lady of Montserrat in Spain, a young girl approached Abbot Millan de Mirando, deeply grieved over her father's recent death.
She begged him to offer three Masses for the repose of his soul, convinced that doing so would free him from the sufferings of purgatory.
Moved by the sincerity of her request, the abbot agreed to celebrate the first Mass the following day.
A Father Seen in Flames
During that first Mass, as the girl knelt near the altar, she reported seeing her father kneeling at its base, surrounded by what she described as frightening flames.

To verify what only she could see, the priest asked her to hold a piece of tissue near the spot where she said the flames were burning — and the tissue, witnesses reported, immediately caught fire on its own.
A White Tunic
At the second Mass, the girl again saw her father, though the flames around him had visibly diminished.

By the third Mass, she described him dressed now in a pure white tunic, and at its conclusion she cried out that she could see him rising, ascending into the sky and passing from her sight for the last time.
Witnesses to the Unseen
Throughout the three Masses, only the girl herself reported seeing her father.
The priests and other witnesses present saw nothing of the vision itself.
Instead, they relied on external, verifiable signs — most notably the burning tissue — to judge whether her account merited belief.
The event was recorded and preserved as testimony to the reality of purgatory and the spiritual value the Church attaches to Masses offered for the dead.
Legacy
The Montserrat account stands apart from most other entries in this exhibition because the Host neither changes nor faces physical threat.
Instead, it centers on the wider power the Church attributes to the Mass, offered even for someone already beyond this life.
Whatever a modern reader makes of a child's private vision three and a half centuries removed, the story has endured at Montserrat.
It remains a specific, concrete illustration of a doctrine — purgatory, and intercession for the dead — that can otherwise remain abstract.
